# From Product to Shape {#sec-product-to-shape}

::: {.chapter-abstract}
Two records bridge the product chain to the geometry, and they point in opposite directions.
Following them is the first thing every reader does and the first place the arrows run the wrong way.
:::

The product chain ends at `#5`, the design definition of the block.
The geometry begins at `#10`, a shape representation.
Nothing in either record refers to the other.
What joins them is a pair of records that Part 41 and Part 43 supply for exactly this purpose:

```step
#3 = SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#4,#10);
#4 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE('','',#5);
#5 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION('design','',#6,#9);
    ...
#10 = ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION('',(#11,#15),#165);
#11 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#12,#13,#14);
#15 = MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP('',#16);
```

Drawn with the arrows as the references actually point:

```default
#5    PRODUCT_DEFINITION ('design')              the part, design view
 ↑
#4    PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE ('','',#5)         "this part has a shape"
 ↑
#3    SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION (#4,#10)   "...and one representation of it"
 │
 ↓
#10   ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION          the container: items + context
 │
 ↓
#15   MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP                          the solid
#11   AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D                          the part's own coordinate frame
```

From the part, the first two hops go *against* the references — `#4` points at `#5`, `#3` points at `#4` — and from `#3` on they run forward.
Every walk from a product to its geometry has this shape: two steps backward, then forward all the way down.
It is the concrete reason a reader needs an index of "who points at me," because the file offers no other way to get from `#5` to `#3`.

## `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` {#sec-product-to-shape-pds}

```step
#4 = PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE('','',#5);
```

The record looks like pure bureaucracy — a name, a description, and "the thing this is the shape of" — and it is, but it is a hook that a surprising amount hangs from.
Its schema:

```express
ENTITY property_definition;
  name        : label;
  description : OPTIONAL text;
  definition  : characterized_definition;
END_ENTITY;

ENTITY product_definition_shape
  SUBTYPE OF (property_definition);
END_ENTITY;
```

`PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` is a *property definition* — the same entity family that carries mass, material and user-defined attributes in @sec-properties-validation — specialised to mean "the shape property."
Its `definition` is a SELECT that may point at a `product_definition`, as here, or at a `next_assembly_usage_occurrence`, which is how a *placement* becomes a shape property of an assembly relationship in the next chapter.
When PMI is present, the tolerance features are `shape_aspects` whose `of_shape` points back at this record.
It is the one node in the product graph that stands for "the geometry of this part, abstractly," and everything that needs to talk about that geometry without naming a specific face attaches here.

## `SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION` {#sec-product-to-shape-sdr}

```step
#3 = SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION(#4,#10);
```

Two attributes: `definition`, the property being represented, and `used_representation`, the representation that does it.
It says: *the shape of this part is represented by `#10`*.

The word *one* matters.
A part may have several `SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION`s, each pointing at the same `PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` and at a different representation: a precise B-rep, a tessellated mesh of the same body, a simplified envelope, or — commonly — a representation containing nothing but an axis placement, so that the part has a coordinate frame even when its geometry is elsewhere.
Readers that take "the first SDR" get the first one the exporter happened to write, which is not always the one wanted.

## The shape representation {#sec-product-to-shape-shape-rep}

```step
#10 = ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION('',(#11,#15),#165);
```

Three attributes, inherited unchanged from Part 43's `representation`: a `name`, the set of `items`, and the `context_of_items`.
This is a **shape representation** — a representation whose items are geometry — and specifically an `ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION`, a subtype that promises its items are B-rep solids built from *advanced* faces (the well-behaved kind, with analytic or B-spline surfaces and fully specified edges).

The subtypes of `SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` are a vocabulary for what kind of geometry to expect:

| Entity type | Items are |
|---|---|
| `SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` | anything — often just an axis placement |
| `ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` | `MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP` solids |
| `MANIFOLD_SURFACE_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` | open shells — surface models |
| `GEOMETRICALLY_BOUNDED_SURFACE_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` | surfaces trimmed by curves, no topology |
| `GEOMETRICALLY_BOUNDED_WIREFRAME_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` | curves only |
| `TESSELLATED_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` | triangle meshes (AP242) |
| `FACETED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION` | solids with planar faces only |

Each subtype has rules about what may appear in `items`; none adds attributes.
For the purposes of walking the file they are all `SHAPE_REPRESENTATION`s, and a reader that wants "the solid" looks for a representation whose items include a `MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP`, whatever the record's type name.

## The items {#sec-product-to-shape-items}

`#10` has two items.

```step
#11 = AXIS2_PLACEMENT_3D('',#12,#13,#14);
#12 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(0.,0.,0.));
#13 = DIRECTION('',(0.,0.,1.));
#14 = DIRECTION('',(1.,0.,-0.));
```

`#11` is an **axis placement**: a point and two directions defining a coordinate frame — origin, Z axis, X axis.
It is the part's own frame, sitting here at the world origin with the identity orientation.
Nearly every shape representation carries one as its first item.
It does not move the geometry; the solid's coordinates are already in this frame.
It exists so that an assembly can say "put the frame of this part at *that* position," and it is what the placement transforms in @sec-assemblies refer to.

```step
#15 = MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP('',#16);
#16 = CLOSED_SHELL('',(#17,#57,#97,#119,#141,#153));
```

`#15` is the solid, and it has one attribute besides its name: the closed shell that bounds it.
The shell lists six faces.
From here down is Part II.

A shape representation can have more than one solid in its items — a part modelled as several disjoint bodies, or a body plus reference geometry.
The clamp's assembly representation in the next chapter has four items and no solids at all: an origin and three placements for the three children.

## Reading the whole path {#sec-product-to-shape-whole-path}

Putting the chapter together, the complete route from "a part called BLOCK" to "a closed shell with six faces" in this file is:

```default
#7  PRODUCT ('BLOCK')
#6  PRODUCT_DEFINITION_FORMATION                <- version
#5  PRODUCT_DEFINITION ('design')               <- view
#4  PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE                    <- shape property   (points UP at #5)
#3  SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION             <- binding  (UP at #4, DOWN at #10)
#10 ADVANCED_BREP_SHAPE_REPRESENTATION          <- container  (-> #165 for units)
#15 MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP
#16 CLOSED_SHELL
#17 ... ADVANCED_FACE x 6
```

Nine records from the part number to the first face, four of which exist only to connect the other five.
It is a lot of indirection for a single block, and the same nine records appear, once per part, in a file with a thousand parts.
But every one of the joints is a place where something else can attach — a second version, a manufacturing view, a tessellated alternative, an assembly placement — and the format pays for that flexibility on every part whether it is used or not.

::: {.callout-important title="In brief"}
`PRODUCT_DEFINITION_SHAPE` points up at the product definition and stands for its shape abstractly.
`SHAPE_DEFINITION_REPRESENTATION` points up at that and down at a shape representation — one of possibly several.
The shape representation's subtype names the kind of geometry; its items are the geometry plus, almost always, an axis placement that is the part's own frame.
Two hops against the arrows, then forward.
:::
